Asphalt in Kennewick Takes a Beating From Both Ends of the Thermometer

Asphalt is a flexible pavement, and its flexibility is exactly what Kennewick's climate attacks. Summer surface temperatures on black asphalt here can push past 150°F, softening the binder until heavy vehicles leave ruts and power-steering scrubs tear the surface — every parking lot in the Tri-Cities has the scars near its drive-throughs. Winter swings the other way: dozens of freeze-thaw cycles work water into every crack, expanding each one a little more per cycle, which is how a hairline crack in October becomes a pothole by March.

The economics of asphalt ownership here follow directly from that: maintenance timing is everything. Crack filling before winter keeps water out of the base; sealcoating every few years replaces the oxidized binder that sun relentlessly strips (UV aging is faster here than the national norm — unprotected asphalt goes gray and brittle years early); and catching base failures small keeps repairs at patch scale instead of reconstruction scale.

Driveways, parking lots, RV pads, private lanes, sealcoating and striping — we can connect you with paving contractors who work the Tri-Cities season, roughly April into October.

Common asphalt paving situations in Kennewick

Sun-bleached, brittle asphalt

Deep black turning gray within a few years is the local UV signature — oxidation cooking the binder out of the surface. Gray asphalt sheds gravel, cracks readily, and absorbs water. Sealcoating on a 3–4 year cycle here (versus 4–5 in kinder climates) is the cheap countermeasure that doubles surface life.

Alligator cracking and soft spots

Interconnected cracking like reptile skin means the base beneath has failed — often from water intrusion through neglected cracks, sometimes from original under-compaction. Surface treatments can't fix a base problem; honest contractors quote dig-out patches for alligatored zones rather than sealing over them.

Edge crumbling on driveways without borders

Asphalt edges unsupported by soil, concrete curb, or compacted shoulder crumble under wheel loads — a top complaint on rural and larger-lot driveways around Kennewick. Edge rebuilds plus backfilled shoulders stop the unraveling; leaving it invites the crumble to walk inward season by season.

How it works

  1. 1

    Evaluation: surface, base, or both

    A contractor walks the pavement, reads the crack patterns, and sorts the job honestly: maintenance (crack fill, sealcoat), repair (patches, overlays), or reconstruction. The crack pattern rarely lies.

  2. 2

    Repairs first

    Cracks routed and hot-filled, failed zones cut out and rebuilt from the base up, drainage corrected where water has been pooling — all before anything cosmetic goes down.

  3. 3

    Sealcoat or overlay

    Sealcoating restores the surface and UV protection on structurally sound asphalt — two coats, applied in warm dry weather (this valley offers plenty). Overlays add new asphalt over aged-but-sound pavement, buying a decade-plus.

  4. 4

    Cure and striping

    Sealcoat cures in 24–48 hours of Kennewick summer; lots reopen fast. Parking lot work finishes with layout and striping — and summer heat means fresh asphalt itself needs gentle treatment (no sharp steering) for its first hot weeks.

What asphalt paving costs in Kennewick

New asphalt in the Tri-Cities prices per square foot with strong scale economies — small driveways cost notably more per foot than lots, since a paving crew and equipment mobilize identically. Sealcoating runs an order of magnitude cheaper per foot, which is the entire argument for maintenance. Crack filling prices per linear foot; patching by the cut-out square footage. Oil prices move asphalt binder cost season to season, so quotes carry shorter shelf lives than concrete bids. The paving season squeeze is real: book major work by spring, because good crews' calendars fill through summer.

Frequently asked questions

Asphalt or concrete for a Kennewick driveway?

Asphalt installs cheaper and tolerates soil movement better; concrete lasts longer with less maintenance and shrugs off 150°F surface days that soften asphalt. In this climate the honest summary: asphalt costs less upfront and demands a maintenance habit; concrete costs more once and mostly leaves you alone.

How often should I sealcoat here?

Every 3–4 years — Kennewick's UV intensity ages binder faster than milder climates, so waiting five-plus years lets oxidation get ahead of you. First sealcoat goes on new asphalt after it cures for a season (6–12 months), not immediately.

Can potholes be fixed in winter?

Cold-patch material can plug a hazard any month, but it's a temporary fix. Proper hot-mix repairs need warm weather and plant production, which locally means roughly April through October. Winter strategy: cold-patch the hazards, list the real repairs for spring.

Why is my asphalt rutting where cars turn?

Heat plus turning loads: soft summer binder scrubbed by power steering, especially where vehicles idle and turn (drive-throughs, garage aprons). Severe rutting may warrant a harder mix or concrete pads at the torture zones — a standard hybrid solution for local lots.

Does sealcoating fix cracks?

No — sealcoat is sunscreen, not surgery. Cracks need routing and rubberized filler first; sealcoat then protects the whole surface. Outfits that spray sealcoat over open cracks are selling appearance; the cracks telegraph back through within months.
